explanation: A stated fact can be pointed to directly: the hook is empty. An inference combines a detail with sensible reasoning: Mara may want the captain’s part because she has polished its buckle and keeps watching its hook. An inference is supported without being stated in exactly those words.

Keep three columns while reading: stated, inferred, and not established. The label passage shows why a plausible guess needs checking. “October” is on the box, but the label alone does not establish a making date for each lantern. Name what a source actually supplies before adding a conclusion.

Decode longer words by looking through the entire spelling, noticing useful parts, and blending them. In unknown, un- means not and known is the base. After decoding, reread the sentence for sense. Do not guess a word merely because its first letter fits your prediction.

passages.title: The Empty Hook
passages.text:
Mara arrived early for the class play. On the wall, a paper label said CAPTAIN beside an empty costume hook. Yesterday Mara had polished the captain’s silver cardboard buckle. Today she carried it in her pocket.
Leo stood near the costume box, winding a strip of cloth around his wrist. He had missed the last rehearsal. Mara opened her mouth, then closed it. She took the buckle out and laid it on the table between them.
“Your sleeve keeps sliding over your hand,” she said. “This cloth might hold it back.”
Leo looked at the buckle. “Ms. Bell asked me to carry the flag. She hasn’t chosen a captain.”
Mara’s shoulders dropped. She laughed once, quietly, and helped him tie the cloth. When Ms. Bell entered, both children were sorting the tangled flags. The captain’s hook was still empty, but Mara no longer watched it.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: What a Label Can Tell Us
passages.text:
A classroom collection contains objects with labels. A useful label gives the object’s name, where it came from, and when that information was recorded. A label is a record, not the object’s complete life story.
Suppose a box is labeled “Paper lanterns, Room 4, October.” The label supports the statement that someone recorded a connection between the lanterns and Room 4. It does not tell who folded every lantern or whether all were made in October. A collector can check a class notebook for those details.
When a label and a notebook disagree, keep both records while asking questions. Perhaps the box was reused; perhaps the notebook describes another batch. Do not silently change one record to fit the other. An honest collection leaves room for information that is still unknown.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

explanation: An inference becomes stronger when two details point in the same direction. Arun moves his backpack off a chair and later makes room near the wide aisle. Together these actions suggest welcome and attention to Bea’s needs. A single spare chair would not show his purpose as clearly.

A main idea covers several details, not just the one you remember best. The clear-path passage includes corners, cupboard doors, and destinations. “A route must work all the way through” explains why those different checks belong together. Avoid turning one successful model into proof about every real user.

Word parts and syllables work together. Re- in reread means again; the whole word still needs accurate sound blending. In arrangement, recognize arrange and -ment, noticing that adding -ment keeps the final e. Read slowly enough to preserve meaning, then repeat the sentence in natural phrases.

examples.prompt: Why does Arun put his backpack on the floor?
examples.answer: He likely wants to keep the extra chair available.
steps: There are six chairs but only five children.
He clears the seat and soon offers a place to Bea.
The actions together support availability more strongly than the chair count alone.

examples.prompt: Why does the cart test not settle everyone’s access needs?
examples.answer: A cart cannot represent every user’s movement.
steps: The passage describes a cart, corners, and cupboard doors.

The class therefore seeks users’ descriptions before deciding.

passages.title: The Spare Chair
passages.text:
At lunch, Arun counted the chairs around his table twice. There were six chairs and five children. He slid the sixth chair away from the crowded aisle, then put his backpack on the floor instead of on its seat.
A new student, Bea, stood at the doorway holding a tray. Arun waved, but she looked toward the far windows. He picked up the spare chair as though he meant to carry it over. Then he noticed her ankle brace and set the chair beside the end of the table, where the aisle was widest.
“Here is a place with plenty of room,” he said. Bea came over. She rested her tray and stretched her foot without bumping anyone.
During lunch, Arun began telling a long joke, forgot its ending, and started laughing anyway. Bea supplied an ending of her own. No one remembered to count the chairs again.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Designing a Clear Path
passages.text:
In this imaginary classroom, students tested two arrangements of desks using an empty cart. In Arrangement A, a straight aisle ended at a bookshelf. To reach the supply cupboard, the cart had to turn around. In Arrangement B, the aisle continued past the bookshelf to the cupboard.
The students recorded more than whether the cart could enter an aisle. They checked its whole route, including corners and the space needed to turn. They also checked that opened cupboard doors did not block the route.
A clear path must connect the places people need to reach. An empty gap beside one desk is not enough if the rest of the route is blocked. The cart test helped students notice obstacles, but it did not represent every person or every way of moving. Before choosing an arrangement, the class invited users of the room to describe what they needed.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

explanation: A topic is a word or phrase such as mistakes or kite making. A theme says something the story suggests about life: a mistake can become a new possibility. Trace the problem, response, and ending before deciding. A theme must fit all three, not just an attractive sentence from outside the story.

Information has a main idea rather than a story’s lesson. The revision record passage explains what a useful record preserves and why. Its paper bridge is an example supporting that idea. A summary should include the record’s purpose while leaving out unnecessary toy details.

Meaningful rereading is not mechanical speed practice. Pause at Nell’s change of mind and compare her first statement with her honest explanation at the display. Decode revision by noticing re- and the ending -sion, pronounced /zhun/ here. Knowing the parts helps you read; the passage supplies the precise meaning.

examples.prompt: Is “kite making” a theme of The Rough Patch?
examples.answer: No; it is a topic.
steps: The phrase names an activity but states no insight.
Nell changes her response to a mistake and acknowledges it.
A theme must express an idea suggested by that change.

examples.prompt: Why is a final photograph an incomplete revision record?
examples.answer: It cannot show the earlier difficulty and all the conditions of the change.
steps: The record includes a first version, difficulty, change, and result.
A final image shows the finished appearance only.
A reader needs the missing sequence to understand what was learned.

passages.title: The Rough Patch
passages.text:
Nell made a paper kite for the windy-day display. She painted a blue river across it and left one corner white. While the paint dried, her little brother accidentally brushed that corner with his wet red sleeve.
Nell snatched up the kite. The red smear looked enormous. “Now it is ruined,” she said. Her brother backed away and held his sleeve behind him.
Nell found fresh paper in a drawer, but the display opened in an hour. She sat beside the damaged kite. The smear forked into three thin lines. Slowly she drew dark branches along them and added a tree leaning over the river. Then she called her brother back.
“Could you hold this edge while I attach the tail?” she asked.
At the display, someone praised the tree. Nell started to say she had planned it. Instead, she said, “That part began with a mistake.” Her brother smiled at the red cuff still visible beneath his coat.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Keeping a Revision Record
passages.text:
A revision record shows how a design changes. It can contain a drawing of the first version, a description of a difficulty, the change made, and the result. It is useful even when a first attempt does not succeed.
For a sample paper bridge, a group first used a flat strip between two supports. The strip bent when a toy car crossed. The group folded the paper into a shallow zigzag and tested the same car across the same gap. This time the paper held the car. This is an invented classroom example, not a claim that any folded bridge will hold any weight.
The record should name what stayed the same as well as what changed. Without that information, a reader cannot tell whether a different car or a shorter gap explains the result. A careful revision record makes learning visible; a photograph of only the final bridge cannot do all that work.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: A Map for the Rain
passages.text:
The walking club planned to follow a chalk map across the playground. Suri had drawn its arrows in three bright colors. She wanted everyone to admire the loop that curled around the climbing frame.
Just before the younger class arrived, rain began to blur the arrows. Suri pressed her umbrella over one perfect curve. Across the yard, Tomas called that the first turn had disappeared.
Suri looked from her beautiful loop to the gate, where the children were waiting. She took a plain piece of cardboard from the supply box and wrote TURN LEFT in large letters. Tomas carried it to the gate. She made two more signs, each simpler than the chalk drawing.
The younger children reached the sheltered porch without getting lost. One asked where the wonderful curly map had gone. Suri smiled sadly at its faded colors, then pointed to the damp group laughing beneath the roof. “It got us started,” she said. “The signs got us here.”
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Summarizing a Set of Directions
passages.text:
Directions for a model library game read: take a number card at the blue desk, wait until that number is called, choose one book from the display, and return the card to the basket. The desk has a yellow lamp and two pots of pencils, but those details do not change the procedure.
A summary of directions should preserve steps whose removal would change what a person does. “Choose a book” is too short because it removes the turn-taking system. “First take a number, wait for it to be called, choose one book, and return the card” preserves the important actions.
The summary should also retain limits. One book is different from as many books as you wish. Descriptive details may be useful for finding a location, however. If there are two desks, “blue desk” could help a reader choose the right one. Whether a detail matters depends on the reader’s task.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: The Unopened Envelope
passages.text:
Jules left a sealed envelope on the rehearsal piano. “For tomorrow,” he told Ada. “Please keep it safe.” Ada placed it beneath the music stand.
Later, she saw Max slip something white into his bag beside the piano. The envelope was no longer under the stand. Ada followed him into the hall. She had already decided what to say when she noticed white paper sticking from a dozen folders on the shelf.
“Did you move an envelope?” she asked.
Max shook his head and pulled a folded schedule from his bag. Together they checked the piano. Beneath a fallen music book lay Jules’s envelope, still sealed. Ada remembered that she had shifted the book while looking for a song.
The next morning she handed Jules his envelope. “It was safe,” she said, then added, “although I nearly solved a mystery that wasn’t there.” Max tapped the schedule in his pocket and grinned.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: When an Observation Has Several Explanations
passages.text:
In a fictional school notebook, a caretaker finds water beside a classroom plant. Three explanations are proposed: someone spilled a watering can, water leaked through a cracked pot, or rain entered an open window. Each is possible before the evidence is checked.
The pot has no visible crack, the window is closed, and the watering can lies on its side. These observations support the spill explanation more strongly than the others. Still, a closed window now does not prove it was closed earlier. Nor does looking for a crack guarantee that every tiny crack would be noticed.
The caretaker records a likely explanation and the observations supporting it. She also records a useful next check: dry the floor, place the upright pot on a tray, and watch for new water. A good explanation can be revised when new evidence appears. Uncertainty does not require treating every explanation as equally likely.

passages.title: The Bench at the Bend
passages.text:
Each morning, Imani passed an old bench at the bend in the school path. One board rattled when she sat down. She wrote BENCH NEEDS REPAIR on a card for the school council and added a picture of a splendid new bench with curved arms.
At the meeting, Mr. Hale explained that the loose board could be secured, but replacing the whole bench would use the group’s entire project fund. Imani folded her drawing. Then Luis said his grandmother needed a place to rest halfway from the gate, before she reached the bend.
The council measured the route and discussed the two locations. Imani unfolded her drawing and turned it over. On the blank side, she drew the old bench with a repaired board and a second, simpler seat near the gate.
A month later she found Luis and his grandmother resting on the new seat. The curved arms from her first drawing were nowhere to be seen. Imani ran her hand along the smooth straight edge and sat beside them.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: A Small Project Decision
passages.text:
This invented council report compares three options for a school path. The group has 100 project tokens, used only as planning units in this example.
Option A: replace the old bench with a decorated bench; cost 100 tokens; one resting place at the bend.
Option B: secure the old bench’s loose board and add a simple seat near the gate; cost 90 tokens; two resting places.
Option C: paint the old bench without repairing its board; cost 20 tokens; one resting place that still needs repair.
The council’s stated goals are a sound seat at the bend and a resting place closer to the gate. Option B meets both goals within the token budget. Cost alone is not the only criterion: C is cheaper, but it leaves the loose board and adds no nearer seat. The report describes these options only; it does not establish the cost of real construction or prove that every user’s needs have been met.

passages.title: The Quiet Rehearsal
passages.text:
The music room was unusually quiet. Mina held two wooden rhythm sticks above her knees while the others unpacked. She had practised the opening beat all weekend, but the room’s sharp echoes made each tap sound enormous.
“Start us off,” said Dev. Mina tapped once and stopped. Dev reached for the sticks. “I can do it.”
Mina held them out, then drew them back. “Could everyone clap softly first?” she asked. The group began a gentle pulse. Mina joined it, first watching the floor, then lifting her eyes toward the circle. When the clapping stopped, her steady taps continued.
After rehearsal, Dev asked why she had changed the opening. “I didn’t change the beat,” Mina replied. “I changed how I got to it.” She packed the sticks in the front pocket of her bag instead of burying them beneath her sweater.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: The Echo Test
passages.text:
In this invented room test, a class claps once in an empty room and hears a clear repeated sound. Then students hang thick fabric panels and repeat the clap from the same marked spot. The repeated sound is less noticeable.
An echo occurs when reflected sound is heard separately from its original sound. Hard surfaces can reflect sound; soft materials can absorb some sound energy. The test description connects a change in the room with a change in what students hear. It does not report exact measurements.
The class keeps the clap location the same to make comparison easier. However, handclaps may differ in loudness, so the observations do not measure how much sound a panel absorbs. A clear explanation names the cause being considered, the observed effect, and the limits of the comparison.

passages.title: The Last Box: A Short Play
passages.text:
Characters: Tess and Omar. Setting: a classroom being packed for a move.
TESS: Everything is in boxes. We can go.
OMAR: [Kneels beside a low cupboard.] Not everything.
TESS: That cupboard is empty.
OMAR: [Reaches beneath it and withdraws a small wooden bird.] Someone forgot this.
TESS: The wings are cracked. Put it in the scrap box.
OMAR: [Turns the bird over.] There is a name underneath: Room 2, first project.
TESS: [Sets down her coat.] I remember sanding those wings. I thought they would never be smooth.
OMAR: Shall I throw it away?
TESS: No. Give me the little box.
[They place folded paper around the bird. Tess writes FIRST PROJECT on the lid.]
OMAR: Now can we go?
TESS: Now we can take the room with us.
[They carry the box out together.]
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Packing a Fragile Object
passages.text:
This practice procedure is for an unsharp wooden model, not broken glass. First inspect the model and choose a box slightly larger than it. Next line the bottom with folded paper. Place the model on the lining without forcing any projecting part against a wall. Add loose folded paper around the sides so the object cannot slide freely. Close the box gently; if the lid presses on the model, choose a deeper box.
Finally label the box with the object’s name and the word FRAGILE. The label helps the next person handle it carefully, but it does not replace padding. The order matters: putting padding only on top after the box is sealed cannot protect the bottom. If a model has a loose part, ask the responsible adult how to secure it before packing.

explanation: Poetry organizes words into lines and often into stanzas. A line ending may invite a light pause, but the sentence can continue across it. Notice the repeated At openings: each begins a different viewpoint. The final stanza moves from seeing objects to considering another person’s perspective.

Comparison structure explains similarities and differences using the same criteria. The article compares lists and sketches by what each preserves well and what each may omit. Do not declare one universally better; choose a form for the purpose. A comparison becomes clearer when both sides answer the same question.

When reading the poem aloud, keep related words together even across a line break. Decode observer from observe and -er, dropping the base’s final e before the vowel-starting suffix. Connect the word’s meaning to a person who notices, then return to the sentence or stanza.

passages.title: Two Windows
passages.text:
At the narrow window
I can see one strip of sky,
a sparrow on the gutter,
a cloud that hurries by.

At the open doorway
I can see the garden wall,
the path beyond the rain barrel,
the shadows growing tall.

At my brother’s shoulder
I can see his drawing grow:
a window wide as morning,
a place I did not know.

I need not trade my window
for the view my brother drew.
I can keep the sky I notice
and make room for his sky, too.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Two Ways to Record a View
passages.text:
An observation list names separate things a viewer notices: one sparrow, a gutter, a cloud. A sketch places shapes in relation to each other. It can show the sparrow above the window or the cloud beyond a roof. Both records can describe a view, but they preserve different information.
Lists make individual entries easy to count or compare. Sketches make position and relative shape easier to see. A sketch may leave out small objects, and a list may leave position unclear unless it adds location words.
A useful record states where the observer stood and when the observation occurred. Views can change with position or time. Neither a list nor a sketch automatically shows everything. Combining a labeled sketch with a short list can preserve both arrangement and details; the reader must still distinguish what was observed from what was imagined.

passages.title: The Door That Stuck
passages.text:
The art-club door swelled during wet weather. Niko pushed it with his shoulder while holding a tray of paper animals. The door sprang open, and a fox slid beneath the table.
“Leave it open,” said Cass. She wedged a folded card under it. Cold air swept through the room, lifting the smaller figures. Niko rescued a rabbit from the floor.
The club considered moving the display to the hall, but the hall table was already used for returned books. Niko set down his tray. “We need to carry fewer things at once,” he said. Cass removed the wedge and held the door while he made two trips. Then they switched jobs.
By the end, every paper animal had reached the shelf. A note beside the handle said PLEASE REPORT THE STICKING DOOR. Niko read it aloud. “Our plan got the animals in,” he said. “It did not fix the door.”

passages.title: A Temporary Plan and a Repair
passages.text:
A temporary plan helps people complete a task while a problem remains. A repair addresses the source of the problem. In the fictional art-club example, having one person hold the door makes carrying supplies easier, but the door still sticks.
A useful problem-and-solution report distinguishes the immediate goal from the long-term goal. Immediate goal: move lightweight paper models without dropping them. Longer-term goal: have a door that opens properly. The report should name who can act on each goal. Students can arrange carrying turns; the responsible building staff decide how to inspect and repair the door.
Record drawbacks as well as benefits. Wedging the door creates a draft in the story, so that proposal causes another difficulty. A successful temporary plan can be worth using without being described as a complete repair.

passages.title: Three Views of a Seed
passages.text:
PROSE: Leda checked her paper cup each morning. On Thursday a green hook broke through the soil. She called her brother, then lowered her voice as if the shoot might be startled. He knelt beside her. Neither touched it.
DRAMA:
LEDA: [Points into the cup.] Look. At last.
SAM: Is that the stem?
LEDA: I think so. Let’s leave it alone.
[They crouch beside the cup, hands behind their backs.]
POEM:
Not a flag,
not a tower,
just a bent green question
in the quiet morning hour.
I lean close,
then lean away;
the smallest guest
has come to stay.
These are three original literary treatments of one imagined event, not a scientific growth record.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Recording a Change Over Time
passages.text:
A fictional student keeps this cup record: Monday—soil surface smooth; Tuesday—no visible change; Wednesday—one small crack in the surface; Thursday—a curved green shoot visible. Each observation is made before lunch from the same side of the cup.
The record presents visible changes in chronological order. It does not show what happened under the soil or during the night. “No visible change” therefore differs from “nothing happened.” A careful observer records what can be seen without adding an unsupported explanation.
A second record could use drawings labeled with the same days. That would make changes in shape easier to compare, but the drawings would still need labels and a consistent viewpoint. The written sequence and labeled pictures could help a reader distinguish an observed change from a guess about its timing or cause.

passages.title: After the First Applause
passages.text:
Scene 1. The puppet curtain fell, and the children behind it bowed to one another. Rafi lifted his cardboard dragon high enough to strike the lamp. The lamp tilted but did not fall. Everyone laughed except Hana, who put one hand around its base.
Scene 2. Before the next show, Hana taped a pale circle on the floor beneath the lamp. “No wings past this line,” she said. Rafi lowered his dragon. He tried a smaller bow and frowned at the tiny movement.
Scene 3. During the show, the audience cheered. Rafi remembered the circle and made his dragon bow sideways, its paper tail curling toward the curtain. The children laughed again, this time at the dragon. Afterward Hana removed the tape while Rafi steadied the lamp. “Same dragon,” he said, “better landing.”
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Three Reports of One Event
passages.text:
These invented reports concern the same rehearsal.
CHRONOLOGY: First a tall puppet struck a lamp. Before the next performance, a boundary was marked. During that performance, the puppet stayed inside the boundary.
CAUSE AND EFFECT: The puppet’s wide upward bow brought it against the lamp. A smaller sideways movement left more clearance, so the lamp was not struck in the next performance.
PROBLEM AND SOLUTION: The performers wanted an expressive bow without hitting nearby equipment. They marked a boundary and practised a different movement. The next performance avoided contact; later performances would need continued care.
The reports select different relationships, not different underlying events. A reader looking for when should consult the chronological account. A reader asking why needs the causal explanation. A reader comparing a difficulty with a response will find the problem-and-solution version most useful.

passages.title: The Golden Paint
passages.text:
I called my paintbrush “Midas” because everything it touched glittered. I painted the cardboard crown, the scenery’s stars, and the handle of the prop broom. Then I painted the little bell we used to signal the curtain.
At rehearsal, I shook the bell. Instead of its bright ring, it gave a dull click. Paint had gathered around the moving part. Asha raised an eyebrow. “Some things need to work more than they need to shine.”
I wanted to argue that the stage looked beautiful. Instead, I put the brush down. We found an unpainted bell in the cupboard. Its plain metal surface looked almost gray beside my crown, but its sound reached the back row.
When someone praised my golden touch, I pointed at the silent bell. “Ask that one first,” I said. I kept it near my paints as a reminder.

passages.title: A Rehearsal Record
passages.text:
This is an original simulation, not a historical document. The stage manager’s later report says: “The rehearsal paused when the painted bell failed to ring clearly. The group replaced it with an unpainted bell. The second bell could be heard from the back row.”
The report was written from a rehearsal log and two participants’ descriptions. It is therefore a secondhand account of the event, even though it includes details from people who were there. It records the practical interruption and solution, but it does not report the painter’s private embarrassment or thoughts.
A first-person account can describe the speaker’s own experience. A secondhand account can combine information from several sources. Neither form automatically guarantees accuracy. Ask how the writer knows each detail and whether a feeling is reported by its owner or inferred by someone else.

passages.title: One Poster, Two Voices
passages.text:
FIRST-PERSON VERSION: I carried the festival poster down the hall with both arms stretched wide. Every time I turned, a corner folded against the wall. “Here comes Atlas,” Noor said. I smiled, but I wished someone would take the other end. When I finally asked, Noor stepped forward at once. The poster became suddenly manageable.
THIRD-PERSON VERSION: Ben carried a broad poster down the hall. Noor saw one corner catch on a doorframe. “Here comes Atlas,” she said, remembering the myth they had read. Ben smiled. Noor thought he was enjoying the joke, so she waited. When he asked for help, she took the far edge. Together they carried the poster flat to the display board.
Both versions are original fiction about the same imagined event. Their narrators reveal different private thoughts.

passages.title: Two Reports of a Delivery
passages.text:
Original simulated firsthand note by the carrier: “The poster was difficult to turn. I did not ask for help until I reached the doorframe. After Noor took the end, we carried it flat.”
Original simulated secondhand school report: “A large poster arrived at the display board without a new fold during the final part of its journey. The report combines the carrier’s note with Noor’s statement that she waited because she thought he wanted to manage alone.”
The firsthand note emphasizes physical difficulty. The secondhand report adds Noor’s stated reason and the delivery result. The sources agree that two people carried the final stretch; neither gives the poster’s measured width.

passages.title: Atlas and the heavens: an excerpt

Atlas, who willingly entered into the arrangement, contrived to put the dragon to sleep, and then, having cunningly outwitted the Hesperides, carried off three of the golden apples, which he now brought to Heracles. But when the latter was prepared to relinquish his burden, Atlas, having once tasted the delights of freedom, declined to resume his post, and announced his intention of being himself the bearer of the apples to Eurystheus, leaving Heracles to fill his place.
passages.attribution: E. M. Berens, Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome, Project Gutenberg edition 2007. Public domain in the USA. Supplied excerpt; page markers omitted.

passages.title: Context for the Atlas excerpt
passages.text: Written for this reading: In the Greek myth recounted by Berens, Atlas supports the heavens on his shoulders. Heracles temporarily takes that burden while Atlas fetches golden apples. passages.title: Behind the Banner
passages.text:
I stood behind the enormous welcome banner while the procession crossed the playground. From my side, I could see shoes, wheels, and the bottoms of bright flags. I heard cheering and assumed everyone had arrived.
“Lift your corner,” Priya whispered. I raised it and saw the last group still waiting at the gate. A younger child was trying to tie a loose shoelace. Priya lowered her corner so I could rest my arms. “They have time,” she said.
Later, I wrote that the procession had stopped because a child needed a moment. Priya read my sentence. “That was one pause,” she said. “There was another before we came outside.”
I added the words while I was watching. They made my sentence longer and my claim smaller. I liked it better that way.

passages.title: Two Parade Notes
passages.text:
These are original simulated records of an imaginary school procession.
Witness note: “From beside the gate, I saw a child stop to tie a shoe. The last group waited briefly, then entered.”
Later report: “The procession paused twice. The indoor organizer recorded a delay while flags were distributed. A gate observer recorded a later pause for a shoelace. No duration was timed.”
The witness gives a direct view of one location. The report combines records from two locations and can describe a wider sequence. However, its writer depends on those records. Briefly is an approximate description, not a measured number of seconds. Readers should preserve that distinction when combining accounts. The report does not tell whether every spectator noticed either pause.

passages.title: The Library Cart
passages.text:
TALIA’S VERSION: I had arranged every book by cover color. The cart looked like a rainbow. When Ren began moving the blue books to different shelves, I felt as though a picture were being torn apart. “Can’t we leave it like this?” I asked.
REN’S VERSION: Talia’s cart was beautiful, but I was looking for the book a younger class had requested. The title began with S. I could not remember its cover. I checked three blue books before finding it among the red ones. I explained our title labels to Talia.
ENDING: Together they put the books on labeled shelves and placed Talia’s rainbow drawing above the cart. The drawing preserved her arrangement without making readers remember cover colors. Talia still liked her picture. Ren now noticed the colors he had first overlooked.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Finding a Book: Two User Accounts

Original simulated firsthand account by a display maker: “The color arrangement attracted children to the cart. Several stopped to look.”

Original simulated secondhand summary: “Two users report different benefits. The display maker emphasizes attention; the searcher emphasizes retrieval, or finding an item again. Their observations can both be true because they address different purposes.”
The summary does not report how many children borrowed a book or how long any search lasted. It distinguishes attracting interest from locating a known item. A reader comparing the accounts should keep those purposes separate before deciding which arrangement suits a particular task.

passages.title: The Race to the Fountain
passages.text:
FIRST PERSON: I reached the fountain breathless. Jo was already there, her hand on the stone rim. I thought she must have taken the shortcut through the garden. I had stayed on the marked path, exactly as we agreed. When she smiled, I looked away.
THIRD PERSON: Jo reached the fountain before Eli. She had stayed on the marked path, but had started while he was still fastening his shoe. When he arrived, she smiled with relief: now they could return the borrowed bucket together. She did not know he thought they were racing.
AFTERWARD: “You won,” Eli said. Jo stared. “Won what?” They compared their memories. Eli had heard “Let’s get there quickly” as a challenge. Jo had meant that the gardener needed the bucket. They walked back at the same pace.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: What a Witness Can and Cannot Establish
passages.text:
A simulated witness says, “I saw Jo arrive before Eli.” That observation establishes an arrival order at one location. It does not establish where either child walked before entering view or whether they had agreed to race.
A simulated later report combines the witness statement with the children’s descriptions. Jo reports following the marked path and starting first. Eli reports believing there was a race. The report distinguishes a shared observation from a difference in understanding.
The words I saw identify a claimed firsthand observation, but a reader must still ask what was visible. A report using third-person names is not automatically impartial or complete. Judge the scope and source of each claim. In these invented records, the witness supports arrival order; the children supply their own intentions and memories.

passages.title: A Herculean Afternoon
passages.text:
“A Herculean task,” Grandad said, surveying the boxes of mixed buttons. Leila imagined lifting a mountain. Then she looked at the tiny buttons and laughed.
Hercules, also called Heracles, is a hero of Greek myth known for difficult feats. Grandad’s phrase meant that sorting the collection would require great effort, not that the buttons were magical or dangerously heavy.
Leila tried making one perfect row by color. By the time she finished the blue buttons, the table was crowded. Her cousin suggested sorting first by size into bowls, then choosing colors within one bowl. Leila disliked abandoning her row, but the bowls left space to work.
That evening Grandad admired the labels. “Finished already?” he asked. Leila shook her head. “Only the coat buttons. We have a good system, though.” She left the small shirt buttons for another day and wrote exactly that on the list.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: The Sorting Log
passages.text:
These are original simulated records. Leila’s firsthand note says, “I found the mixed pile overwhelming. Size bowls helped me work on one group at a time. We completed the coat buttons.” Her cousin’s note says, “I suggested bowls because the row covered the table. We left the shirt buttons unsorted.”
A later summary could combine the notes: the pair changed the organization to make workspace and completed one part of the collection. It should not say the entire collection was finished. Both notes limit the result, though one emphasizes feelings and the other emphasizes space.
In a task log, completed should identify a specific scope. A progress record is useful when it tells the next worker what remains. Precise limits can coexist with pride in the work already accomplished.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.text:
The rehearsal room was crowded when Nessa reached the door. She held a folded script against her chest. Cal moved a stool away from the doorway.
“Come in,” he said. “There is room.”
Nessa looked at the cleared space, then at the circle of readers. She opened the script and took the stool. Cal waited until she found the page before beginning again.

Version B—snap the invitation impatiently, pull the stool roughly, and begin again before she opens the script. Perform both versions with voices or read these directions as a performance transcript. No recording is required.

Monday | 8 | 8
Tuesday | 10 | 8
Wednesday | 9 | 9

passages.title: Before the Bell
passages.text:
One coat slides from its peg.
One chair scrapes back.
One pencil rolls
along a crack.

Then quiet gathers,
small and slow;
we hear the clock,
we let it go.

The bell will ring.
It has not yet.
There is a breath
we need not fret.

Performance A: read the first stanza briskly, then slow through the pauses in the next two. Performance B: read every line at one rapid pace without pausing at sentence endings. Try both aloud. Fret means worry. The poem is an imagined classroom moment, not advice about a real emergency.

passages.title: Settling Time

A fictional class records how long it takes to put supplies away and become ready for a quiet reading period.
Day | Minutes from signal to readiness
Monday | 5
Tuesday | 4
Wednesday | 4
Thursday | 3
The class practises a shared cleanup routine during these days. The author says the record is consistent with quicker settling, because Thursday’s time is shorter than Monday’s. The times do not become shorter every day: Tuesday and Wednesday match.
This record alone cannot prove the routine caused the change. Different tasks or different numbers of people could matter, and those conditions were not recorded. It supports a description of the observed pattern. To investigate an explanation, the class would need more information about the conditions and additional observations.

passages.title: The Long Way Round
passages.text:
“The hall is quicker,” said Kit. Jo looked at the paper boats balanced on their tray. Beyond the hall doors, a running game had just begun. Jo pointed toward the quiet library corridor.
Kit sighed, then followed. At the library window they stopped while a class passed. A younger child admired the boats and asked where they were going. Kit’s answer grew into a story about their imaginary harbor.
They reached the display room after the hall group, but every boat remained upright. “We missed the race,” Kit said. Then he looked at the tray. “Perhaps we weren’t in it.”
Performance directions: play Kit’s first line eagerly, his sigh impatiently, and his final line thoughtfully. Jo should point before moving; no narrator claims Jo is afraid. Perform or orally describe these choices and compare them with the written scene.

Hall route: classroom → hall → display room. Length 20 meters. During the game, runners use the hall.
Library route: classroom → library corridor → display room. Length 32 meters. Walking groups use the corridor.
The guide recommends the library route for carrying delicate models while the game is underway. It is 12 meters longer but avoids the running area. It does not promise an empty corridor: walking groups may still pass. No travel times or accident counts are supplied.
A route diagram supplies order and connections; its length labels supply distance. Distance alone cannot establish travel time when people may stop or move at different speeds. Choose a route by considering the stated purpose and the conditions, not just the shortest line.

passages.title: The Last Invitation: A Play
passages.text:
[A club table holds three invitation designs.]
MIRA: This one has the most glitter.
SOL: Can you read the meeting time?
MIRA: [Tilts the card.] Not from here.
SOL: Try this plain one.
MIRA: Friday, three o’clock. It looks rather empty.
SOL: There is space for a picture above the words.
[Mira draws a small comet without covering the time.]
MIRA: Now it looks like our astronomy club.
SOL: And people will know when to come.
Performance trial: first read Sol as scolding; then read Sol as curious and practical. Keep the same words. Discuss which delivery is more consistent with suggesting space for Mira’s picture, and identify any uncertainty. These are classroom interpretations, not recordings of an actual meeting.

passages.title: Which Invitation Communicates?
passages.text:
An original classroom trial uses three imaginary designs. Each is shown to the same six readers from a marked distance.
Design | Readers who correctly read the time
Glitter over words | 2 of 6
Plain large words | 6 of 6
Large words with separate comet | 6 of 6
The writer recommends keeping decoration separate from essential words. The two designs with unobstructed large words had all six readers identify the time, while the glitter-covered version had only two.
This small trial supports a choice for these cards and readers. It does not prove every decoration interferes with reading or that size alone caused the result; placement and other design differences may also matter. The recommendation combines readability with room for a meaningful picture, rather than treating plainness as the only possible goal.

passages.title: The Applause Jar
passages.text:
The class placed a pebble in a jar whenever a rehearsal ended with every prop returned. On Friday the jar looked fuller than it had on Monday. Evan held it toward the light.
“We are the most organized class anywhere,” he announced.
Rosa smiled. “We returned our props four times this week. That is good.” She pointed at the floor, where a scarf lay beneath a chair. Evan picked it up and folded it.
“For today,” he said, “we still have work.”
Performance A: Evan begins with a boast and ends thoughtfully; Rosa is friendly and exact. Performance B: Rosa laughs cruelly and Evan storms out without collecting the scarf. Read or perform both and identify which changes are interpretations and which contradict the written action.

passages.title: A Rehearsal Checklist
passages.text:
This fictional weekly display records completed cleanup checks, not a ranking of classes.
Day | Props returned? | Floor checked?
Monday | yes | yes
Tuesday | yes | no
Wednesday | no | yes
Thursday | yes | yes
Friday | yes | no
Four days have props returned; three days have the floor checked. Only Monday and Thursday meet both checks. The author recommends using two checkboxes because one completed task can hide another unfinished one.
The display supports that recommendation: Tuesday and Friday show returned props without a completed floor check. It does not record how many props were used, whether a later check corrected an omission, or what other classes did. A clear report names the measure before praising progress.

passages.title: The Lantern Line
passages.text:
At the end of the display, Mei found that her lantern hung lower than the others. She reached to pull its cord higher, but Tomas stopped her.
“Look from the doorway,” he said.
From there, the lanterns made a gentle slope, each slightly lower than the one before. Mei’s lantern completed the line. She stood quietly, then let the cord fall back into place.
“I was measuring it against the wrong neighbor,” she said.
Two performance plans: Plan A—Mei begins hurriedly, walks to the doorway, studies the whole line, and relaxes her hand. Plan B—Mei angrily cuts every cord until all lanterns fall. Perform Plan A or read its actions aloud, then explain what Plan B changes. These are paper display lanterns; no flame or electrical work is involved.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Viewing the Whole Display
passages.text:
An invented display plan lists lantern heights above the floor.
Position from left | Height in centimeters
1 | 160
2 | 150
3 | 140
4 | 130
The designer wants a steady descending line from left to right. Each neighboring height decreases by 10 centimeters. A viewer examining position 4 alone might call it too low; the full pattern explains its intended role.
The author recommends checking both individual placement and the whole arrangement before changing a display. This table supports the planned pattern, not a claim that everyone will prefer it. It also does not show the actual cords or verify that the installed lanterns match the plan. To check installation, someone would need actual height measurements taken from the same floor reference.

passages.title: Labam quest: the departure
passages.text:
At last he told his father and mother that he wanted to go and see the Princess Labam. "I must go," he said; "I must see what she is like. Tell me where her country is."

"We do not know where it is," answered his father and mother.

"Then I must go and look for it," said the prince.

"No, no," they said, "you must not leave us. You are our only son. Stay with us. You will never find the Princess Labam."

"I must try and find her," said the prince. "Perhaps God will show me the way. If I live and I find her, I will come back to you; but perhaps I shall die, and then I shall never see you again. Still I must go."

So they had to let him go, though they cried very much at parting with him. His father gave him fine clothes to wear, and a fine horse. And he took his gun, and his bow and arrows, and a great many other weapons, "for," he said, "I may want them." His father, too, gave him plenty of rupees.

Then he himself got his horse all ready for the journey, and he said good-bye to his father and mother; and his mother took her handkerchief and wrapped some sweetmeats in it, and gave it to her son. "My child," she said to him, "When you are hungry eat some of these sweetmeats."

passages.title: Planning Notes A and B
passages.text:
Text A—A supply plan separates what a traveler needs from how it is carried. List food, water, clothing, and any task materials. Identify which items are already available and which need preparation. A list alone does not show that items are packed.
Text B—A packing check names the container and checks that the traveler can manage its weight. Place needed items where they can be reached and label shared bags so their owners can identify them. Check the actual contents against the supply list before leaving.
These original instructional texts complement each other. A identifies needs and readiness; B checks carrying and contents. Neither gives a universal quantity of food or water. Those amounts depend on a real journey’s conditions, which this general reading does not supply.

passages.title: Momotaro quest: leaving home
passages.text:
“All you say is very interesting, Momotaro,” said the old man. “I will not hinder you in your determination. You may go if you wish. Go to the island as soon as ever you like and destroy the demons and bring peace to the land.”

“Thank you, for all your kindness,” said Momotaro, who began to get ready to go that very day. He was full of courage and did not know what fear was.

The old man and woman at once set to work to pound rice in the kitchen mortar to make cakes for Momotaro to take with him on his journey.

At last the cakes were made and Momotaro was ready to start on his long journey.

Parting is always sad. So it was now. The eyes of the two old people were filled with tears and their voices trembled as they said:

“Go with all care and speed. We expect you back victorious!”

Momotaro was very sorry to leave his old parents (though he knew he was coming back as soon as he could), for he thought of how lonely they would be while he was away. But he said “Good-by!” quite bravely.

“I am going now. Take good care of yourselves while I am away. Good-by!” And he stepped quickly out of the house. In silence the eyes of Momotaro and his parents met in farewell.

passages.title: Labam quest: the ants
passages.text: He then set out on his journey, and rode on and on till he came to a jungle in which were a tank and shady trees. He bathed himself and his horse in the tank, and then sat down under a tree. "Now," he said to himself, "I will eat some of the sweetmeats my mother gave me, and I will drink some water, and then I will continue my journey." He opened his handkerchief, and took out a sweetmeat. He found an ant in it. He took out another. There was an ant in that one too. So he laid the two sweetmeats on the ground, and he took out another, and another, and another, until he had taken them all out; but in each he found an ant. "Never mind," he said, "I won't eat the sweetmeats; the ants shall eat them." Then the Ant-Raja came and stood before him and said, "You have been good to us. If ever you are in trouble, think of me and we will come to you."

passages.title: An Offer and a Receipt
passages.text:
Text A—An offer record states who is willing to provide a resource, what is offered, and any condition attached. “I can bring two empty boxes if someone collects them” records a conditional offer. It does not establish that the boxes have arrived.
Text B—A receipt record states what was actually received and when. “One empty box received on Tuesday” confirms one arrival. It does not automatically cancel a larger offer; the remaining box may still be expected.
In this invented example, combining A and B shows that two boxes were offered conditionally but one is recorded as received. A careful summary distinguishes promise, condition, and outcome. To know what happened to the second box, a reader would need another record rather than a guess.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Momotaro quest: a follower joins
passages.text:
“I think I can take you with me if you wish to go,” said Momotaro.

“Thank you!” said the dog. “By the way, I am very very hungry. Will you give me one of the cakes you are carrying?”

“This is the best kind of cake there is in Japan,” said Momotaro. “I cannot spare you a whole one; I will give you half of one.”

“Thank you very much,” said the dog, taking the piece thrown to him.

Then Momotaro got up and the dog followed. For a long time they walked over the hills and through the valleys. As they were going along an animal came down from a tree a little ahead of them. The creature soon came up to Momotaro and said:

“Good morning, Momotaro! You are welcome in this part of the country. Will you allow me to go with you?”

passages.title: Making a Working Agreement
passages.text:
Text A—A group agreement names what members will do. “We will listen without interrupting while a person describes a problem” is more specific than “We will be good.” A useful agreement also identifies how the group will pause and repair a disagreement.
Text B—A role chart identifies who carries each task and when roles change. It can prevent two people from assuming the other has done a job. A chart does not by itself guarantee respectful behavior; people must still follow the agreement.
These original instructional texts address different needs. A describes interaction; B describes responsibility. Combining them can clarify both conduct and work, but neither promises that a written rule will eliminate every disagreement. A group must observe whether its plan is actually followed.

passages.title: Momotaro quest: an agreement
passages.text:
Then Momotaro stood and gave this order:

“Now all of you must listen to me. The first thing necessary in an army is harmony. It is a wise saying which says that ‘Advantage on earth is better than advantage in Heaven!’ Union amongst ourselves is better than any earthly gain. When we are not at peace amongst ourselves it is no easy thing to subdue an enemy. From now, you three, the dog, the monkey and the pheasant, must be friends with one mind. The one who first begins a quarrel will be discharged on the spot!”

All the three promised not to quarrel. The pheasant was now made a member of Momotaro’s suite, and received half a cake.

Momotaro’s influence was so great that the three became good friends, and hurried onwards with him as their leader.

passages.title: A Route Plan and a Travel Account
passages.text:
Text A—A route plan can name connected places and the order of stops. For an invented trip: home → bridge → harbor → island. The arrows show planned order, not distance, speed, or what a traveler feels. If a distance is needed, the plan must supply a labeled measurement.
Text B—A travel account can describe events along a route: waiting at the bridge, feeling uneasy on a boat, or noticing calm weather. It may omit distances even when the writer remembers the journey vividly. A reader should distinguish an actual observation from a feeling or an imagined comparison.
Combined, the texts explain why a map and an account answer different questions. A mapped connection does not prove a journey occurred, and a vivid story does not automatically provide exact geography.

passages.title: Momotaro quest: across the sea
passages.text: Momotaro now got a small ship, and they all got on board. The wind and weather were fair, and the ship went like an arrow over the sea. It was the first time they had ever been on the water, and so at first the dog, the monkey and the pheasant were frightened at the waves and the rolling of the vessel, but by degrees they grew accustomed to the water and were quite happy again. Every day they paced the deck of their little ship, eagerly looking out for the demons’ island.

passages.title: Labam quest: the mustard-seed task
passages.text:
The prince was very sorry when he heard this. "How can I crush the oil out of all this mustard seed in one day?" he said to himself; "and if I do not, the king will kill me." He took the mustard seed to the old woman's house, and did not know what to do. At last he remembered the Ant-Raja, and the moment he did so, the Ant-Raja and his ants came to him. "Why do you look so sad?" said the Ant-Raja.

The prince showed him the mustard seed, and said to him, "How can I crush the oil out of all this mustard seed in one day? And if I do not take the oil to the king to-morrow morning, he will kill me."

"Be happy," said the Ant-Raja; "lie down and sleep; we will crush all the oil out for you during the day, and to-morrow morning you shall take it to the king." The Raja's son lay down and slept, and the ants crushed out the oil for him. The prince was very glad when he saw the oil.

passages.title: Requirement and Resource
passages.text:
Text A—For an invented paper-model task, the requirement is to move a paper message from one desk to another without letting it touch the floor. The task does not require speed or a decorative design. A successful result must be checked against the stated condition.
Text B—Available materials are string, paper clips, and folded cards. String can connect the desks; clips can attach a card to the string. This list describes possible resources, not a finished tested solution. The distance between desks and the strength of attachments would need checking before choosing a design.
Together, these texts suggest matching a resource’s useful property to an actual requirement. A tool that looks impressive may not address the obstacle. A proposed plan still needs a check; a material list alone cannot establish success.

passages.title: Momotaro quest: a winged helper
passages.text:
Momotaro knew at once that what they saw was the devils’ stronghold. On the top of the precipitous shore, looking out to sea, was a large castle. Now that his enterprise was close at hand, he was deep in thought with his head leaning on his hands, wondering how he should begin the attack. His three followers watched him, waiting for orders. At last he called to the pheasant:

“It is a great advantage for us to have you with us.” said Momotaro to the bird, “for you have good wings. Fly at once to the castle and engage the demons to fight. We will follow you.”

passages.title: Labam quest: the final aid and return
passages.text:
Then she pulled out a hair from her head, and gave it to the prince. "To-morrow," she said, "when no one is near you, you must say to the tree-trunk, 'The Princess Labam commands you to let yourself be cut in two by this hair.' Then stretch the hair down the edge of the wax hatchet's blade."

The prince next day did exactly as the princess had told him; and the minute the hair that was stretched down the edge of the hatchet-blade touched the tree-trunk it split into two pieces.

The king said, "Now you can marry my daughter." Then the wedding took place. All the Rajas and kings of the countries round were asked to come to it, and there were great rejoicings. After a few days the prince's son said to his wife, "Let us go to my father's country." The Princess Labam's father gave them a quantity of camels and horses and rupees and servants; and they travelled in great state to the prince's country, where they lived happily.

passages.title: Source Notes A and B
passages.text:
Text A—The Labam selections come from Joseph Jacobs’s Indian Fairy Tales, published in 1892. The provided text is an English collected version. Its title, collector, and edition help a reader identify which version is being discussed. The ending prints “the prince’s son” after following the prince and his bride; that wording is preserved, but the excerpt introduces no separate child. Do not build an additional family history from it. An edition date is not the date of every event imagined in the tale.
Text B—The Momotaro selections come from Yei Theodora Ozaki’s Japanese Fairy Tales, in the linked Project Gutenberg edition released in 2003. That digital release date does not mean the traditional tale began in 2003. These weekly selections omit parts of each complete work; they support analysis of the supplied episodes, not claims that every scene has been studied.
Together the notes encourage precise attribution and modest scope. Two selected versions can show a shared quest pattern and distinctive details. They cannot stand for every Indian or Japanese tradition or certify comprehensive reading of either collection.

passages.title: Momotaro quest: the return
passages.text:
The dog and the pheasant carried home the plunder, and thus Momotaro returned triumphantly to his home, taking with him the devil chief as a captive.

The two poor damsels, daughters of Daimios, and others whom the wicked demon had carried off to be his slaves, were taken safely to their own homes and delivered to their parents.

The whole country made a hero of Momotaro on his triumphant return, and rejoiced that the country was now freed from the robber devils who had been a terror of the land for a long time.

The old couple’s joy was greater than ever, and the treasure Momotaro had brought home with him enabled them to live in peace and plenty to the end of their days.

passages.title: The Cabinet Project, Chapter 1: The Card
passages.text:
The cabinet at the end of the school library had always held a jumble of models, photographs, and curled paper signs. When the librarian invited Class Four to make a small exhibit, everyone reached for the brightest objects. Noor chose a faded card with a blue border. Across its top someone had written FIRST GARDEN DAY. No year followed the words.
“That must be when the school opened,” Ben said. He was already drawing a large title for the exhibit: OUR FIRST DAY.
Noor turned the card over. On the back were six names, two crossed out and rewritten. “Maybe,” she said. “Or maybe the garden began later.”
Ben pressed harder with his pencil. He liked a title that sounded important. The librarian, Ms. Vega, brought a thin folder to their table. Inside were three photocopied notices and a photograph of children carrying empty flowerpots. A note beneath the photograph read SPRING FAIR, but it did not name a year either.
Noor spread the papers out without covering their edges. “We could find out what they actually tell us.”
“Then our title would be very small,” Ben said.
“Small enough to be true.” Noor expected him to laugh, but he looked at the crowded cabinet instead. On its lowest shelf stood a wooden bird with a chipped beak. Someone had carefully tied a string around its broken wing.
Ben erased OUR FIRST DAY. Beneath the pale marks, he wrote a question: HOW DID PEOPLE USE THIS SPACE?
Noor nodded. The question was large enough to include the objects and small enough to investigate. They put the blue card in a sleeve and started a list, leaving a wide empty column headed STILL UNKNOWN.
passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original classroom reading.

passages.title: Cabinet Records A and B
passages.text:
All records in this six-week project are original simulations for a fictional school, not authentic historical documents.
Record A—Card transcript: “FIRST GARDEN DAY.” Reverse: six participant names, including two corrected entries. No year or school-opening statement appears. The transcript preserves wording but not the card’s exact color or dimensions.
Record B—Photograph description: several children carry empty flowerpots beside a doorway. Caption: “SPRING FAIR.” No date is visible. A photograph can preserve visible arrangement, but the supplied description cannot identify the people or establish why the pots are empty.
Together the records support a gardening-related school activity and a fair-related image. They do not establish that the events occurred together, that either marked the school’s opening, or that the card’s names belong to the photographed children. Those are questions for further evidence.

passages.title: The Cabinet Project, Chapter 2: The Narrow Shelf
passages.text:
Noor and Ben’s question—HOW DID PEOPLE USE THIS SPACE?—stood at the top of a blank exhibit board. Their first objects were an undated garden card, a fair photograph, and a wooden bird with a repaired wing. They had agreed to mark unknown facts clearly. Now they had to decide how the objects would fit.
Ben drew a tall platform for the bird. From across the library, it would look as though the little creature were taking flight. Noor measured the shelf below the board. “A platform will hide the card,” she said.
“Put the card behind it. People can lean over.”
Ms. Vega brought two chairs. “Try looking from here.” Sitting down, Ben could see the bird but almost none of the card. He shifted sideways, then leaned so far that his sketch slipped from his knee.
Noor did not say she had been right. She turned the sketch around. “The raised part could go at the back. The card could lie at the front.”
They made paper stand-ins and tested the arrangement. Ben read the card easily from the first chair. From the second, light reflected off its clear sleeve and hid the word GARDEN. They tilted the sleeve and tried again. This time the glare moved away from the lettering.
By lunch, the grand flying platform had become a plain low support. Ben placed his unused sketch in the project folder rather than throwing it away. Beneath it he wrote: A GOOD IDEA FOR ONE VIEW CAN BE A BAD IDEA FOR ANOTHER.
Noor added a smaller note: CHECK MORE THAN ONE VIEW. Neither note called the exhibit finished.

passages.title: Display Sources A and B
passages.text:
Source A—Fictional shelf plan: the card lies at the front, the bird stands on a low support behind it, and the caption board rises at the back. A sightline is the straight direction from a viewer’s eye toward an object. The plan aims to keep the bird from blocking the card along a seated viewer’s sightline.
Source B—Fictional trial note: chair 1, card words visible; chair 2, sleeve glare hides GARDEN. After a slight sleeve tilt, both seated test viewers can read the whole card. The note concerns these positions and this lighting only.
A describes the planned arrangement; B records a limited check. Together they support retaining the low support and tilted sleeve for the tested conditions. They do not establish that every viewer, every height, or every future lighting condition will work equally well.

passages.title: The Cabinet Project, Chapter 3: Two Blue Ribbons
passages.text:
The exhibit now used a low bird support and a tilted card sleeve so seated readers could see the words. Dates were still missing from the garden card and fair photograph. Noor hoped that interviews would fill the empty column.
Mr. Chen remembered tying a blue ribbon across the garden gate before a celebration. Ms. Ortiz remembered a blue ribbon around a bundle of paper invitations. “We made them in the old art room,” she said.
Ben immediately wrote: THE BLUE RIBBON OPENED THE GARDEN.
Noor touched the pencil’s eraser. “There may have been two ribbons.”
Mr. Chen studied the photocopied photograph. “I remember a gate, but this picture shows a doorway. I cannot tell you whether it was the same day.” Ms. Ortiz added that her invitations might have been made for a later fair. Neither sounded embarrassed by the uncertainty.
Ben had expected memories to fit like puzzle pieces with smooth edges. Instead, each answer seemed to create another question. He turned the interview sheet sideways, as if a different angle might help.
Noor drew two boxes. In one she wrote GATE RIBBON. In the other she wrote INVITATION RIBBON. Between them she placed a dotted line and the words POSSIBLE CONNECTION.
“That makes our exhibit look unfinished,” Ben said.
“It is unfinished,” Noor replied. “The events are over. Our finding out is not.”
At the next meeting, Ben read each person’s words aloud before offering his own explanation. He left the dotted line on the board. For the first time, the empty space looked less like failure and more like an invitation.

passages.title: Interview Records A and B
passages.text:
These are original simulated interviews with fictional participants.
A—Mr. Chen: “I tied a blue ribbon across a garden gate before a celebration. I cannot tell whether the supplied doorway photograph shows that same day.”
B—Ms. Ortiz: “I remember blue ribbon around a bundle of paper invitations made in the old art room. They might have been for a later fair.”
Both accounts connect blue ribbon with preparations, but they identify different objects and locations. They can both be true if there were two ribbons or two occasions. The records do not prove that explanation, however. Nor do they establish that one person must be wrong.
A combined exhibit note should attribute each memory and keep the relationship unresolved. Color agreement alone is weak evidence of object identity. Another dated record, a labeled photograph, or a clearer participant account could help test the possible connection.

passages.title: The Cabinet Project, Chapter 4: Three Visitors
passages.text:
The group’s board now included two separate ribbon memories joined by a dotted line. Noor and Ben decided to test whether visitors understood that the connection was uncertain. They invited three classmates, one at a time, to look at a paper version of the exhibit.
The first visitor traced the dotted line. “These are definitely the same ribbon,” she said.
Ben glanced at Noor. The second visitor read the labels aloud and shrugged. “Maybe the same event, maybe not.” The third did not notice the dotted line at all. He admired the wooden bird and asked who had repaired its wing.
“We need a bigger question mark,” Ben said.
Noor held up the first visitor’s note. “Or words that say what we mean.”
They replaced POSSIBLE CONNECTION with WE DO NOT YET KNOW WHETHER THESE MEMORIES DESCRIBE THE SAME OCCASION. Ben worried that the sentence was too long. He read it aloud, paused after know, and discovered that it sounded clear in two parts.
For the next trial, they kept the pictures and positions the same and changed only that label. All three new visitors said the connection was uncertain. One still asked about the bird’s wing, which remained a separate question.
Their trial sheet ended with a note: SIX VISITORS ARE NOT EVERY VISITOR.
Performance task: read Ben’s long label first without a pause, then with the meaning-preserving pause he chose. Explain how the pause helps without changing the evidence claim.

passages.title: The Cabinet Project, Chapter 5: The Missing Name
passages.text:
The clearer ribbon label was ready, and the bird stood behind the garden card without hiding it. One question remained beside the bird: WHO REPAIRED THE WING? Ben wanted a name before opening day. He thought an exhibit with so many question marks might look careless.
Noor found a repair list in the folder. It named three objects but no repairers: a frame, a stool, and a wooden bird. Beside the bird was a short note—THREAD REPLACED; WING STILL FRAGILE.
“That must be Ms. Vega,” Ben said. “She knows where everything is.”
Ms. Vega looked at the list and shook her head. “I put this sheet in the folder. I did not write it.”
For a moment Ben felt the old disappointment return. Then he noticed something he had not asked before. “What can we say, even without the name?”
Noor placed the bird’s old photograph beside it. In the photograph, the wing hung lower and the thread was dark. On the shelf, the wing sat higher and pale thread looped around it.
They wrote: THE REPAIR LIST RECORDS REPLACED THREAD. THE PHOTOGRAPH AND OBJECT SHOW DIFFERENT WING POSITIONS. THE REPAIRER’S NAME IS NOT RECORDED HERE.
Ben read the caption twice. It did not sound careless. It sounded as though somebody had looked closely.
Before leaving, he added a small card below it: DO YOU HAVE INFORMATION ABOUT THIS REPAIR? PLEASE TELL THE LIBRARIAN HOW YOU KNOW. This time the question mark felt like part of the exhibit, not a hole in it.

passages.title: The Cabinet Project, Chapter 6: Opening Day
passages.text:
On opening morning, Ben arrived carrying the first title he had drawn weeks before: OUR FIRST DAY. Its letters were bold, and the rubbed-out pencil marks around them made a pale cloud. He placed it in the project folder beside the flying-platform sketch. Neither had become part of the exhibit, but both explained how the exhibit had changed.
The final board asked HOW DID PEOPLE USE THIS SPACE? Below it, the undated garden card rested in its tilted sleeve. The fair photograph had its own label, without a claim that it showed the same day. Two ribbon memories were printed separately, joined by words that explained the uncertain connection. The wooden bird’s caption reported replaced thread and a still-fragile wing, without inventing a repairer.
Noor stood beside the board as the first visitors entered. One child wanted to know why the labels included so many things the class did not know.
“Because we wanted you to see what the records say,” Ben answered, “and where another record could change our minds.”
A visitor brought a note describing a possible repairer. Noor thanked her and asked how she knew. The visitor had heard the story from a friend, so they put the note in a folder marked LEADS TO CHECK rather than rewriting the caption at once.
Later, when the library grew quiet, Ben looked at the bird. Its pale thread was easy to miss unless you stood close. “It is a small exhibit,” he said.
Noor looked from the card to the photograph, from the careful labels to the new folder. “It has room to grow.”
They closed the cabinet gently. The question at the top remained open, not because their work had failed, but because they had learned how to continue.

Source B—New lead form: a visitor names a possible repairer based on a story from a friend. The friend’s original account has not been obtained. The form records the visitor as the immediate source and marks the claim unverified. It proposes asking the friend what was directly observed or learned from another person.
Together the sources show why the current caption should remain while the new lead is investigated. Unverified does not mean false; it means this dossier does not yet establish the claim. A final report can be complete about its present findings while still identifying a useful next question.
